I farm 6 mu, and I do not start from zero. I look first at what has held yield for me in this county: cabbage needs steady water and heavy feeding, maize can carry the field through summer if I do not starve it early, chili and kidney bean give me cash and food but I will not let them take too much land from the main cabbage-maize-cabbage rotation, and spinach is quick so I use it where I can fit it. Because I have well irrigation, I will push vegetables a bit harder than dryland farmers do. My education is high and I have farmed 40 years, so I think in terms of yield target and nutrient balance, but I still keep one eye on cost. Nitrogen drives leaf growth, especially for cabbage and spinach, but if I push only nitrogen, the crop gets soft and disease comes easier, so I will keep phosphorus and potassium up too. On my 6 mu, I would rather spend somewhat more on fertilizer than lose a harvest, especially on cabbage. I will keep plough tillage before the first cabbage to bury residue and manure well, then mostly use rotary tillage between later crops to save labor and water. For pesticides, I will not spray on a calendar only; still, in a normal year, cabbage and chili need more passes, maize and bean less. My plan this year is to keep the main area in spring cabbage, follow with summer maize on most of that land, then return to autumn cabbage, while holding smaller areas for chili, kidney bean, and spinach so the household has diversity and some cash flow.
